questions.question: The Brundtland definition of sustainable development is:
options: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Development that maximises this decade's GDP
Development funded only by renewable industries
Development that stays within one region

questions.question: A remote Karoo village is better served by solar panels and a borehole pump than by connection to a distant national mega-plant. This illustrates:
options: Economic development
Appropriate-scale development — the solution matched to local skills, budgets and needs
Spatial development
Mass consumption

questions.question: The five aspects of development named in the lesson are:
options: Primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary
Local, regional, national, continental and global
Economic, social, sustainable, appropriate-scale and spatial
Health, education, income, trade and aid

questions.question: Social development is described as converting money into lives because:
options: It measures bank deposits
It replaces economic development entirely
It applies only to cities
It turns economic gains into education, health care, housing, safe water and the inclusion of women — outcomes rather than output

questions.question: The backwash effect describes:
options: The periphery's young, skilled people and its capital draining toward the core, leaving the periphery less able to catch up
Investment flowing from core to periphery
Flooding in low-lying regions
The decline of the core as costs rise

questions.question: Cumulative causation is the model's engine because:
options: Government decrees where factories must locate
Success attracts success — a factory draws suppliers, workers and taxes, funding infrastructure that attracts the next factory
All regions grow at the same rate
Raw materials always stay in the periphery

questions.question: At the national scale, South Africa's clearest core-periphery pair is:
options: The Western Cape core and Gauteng periphery
Durban core and Johannesburg periphery
Gauteng — about a third of GDP on the smallest provincial footprint — as core, with former homeland districts of the Eastern Cape and Limpopo as periphery
The coast as core and the entire interior as periphery

questions.question: Spread effects are:
options: The expansion of the core's boundaries
The growth of informal settlements
Diseases moving along transport routes
Investment, remittances and demand flowing from core to periphery — the flows planners try to strengthen

questions.question: The correct order of Rostow's five stages is:
options: Traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption
Take-off, preconditions, maturity, tradition, consumption
Traditional society, take-off, preconditions, consumption, maturity
Preconditions, traditional society, take-off, consumption, maturity

questions.question: Take-off is marked by:
options: The end of all farming
Rapid growth of manufacturing with investment climbing past roughly 10 per cent of national income, so growth becomes self-sustaining
The arrival of foreign aid
Services overtaking industry

questions.question: The criticism that connects Rostow's model to colonial history is:
options: Britain never actually industrialised
Colonies took off before their colonisers
Britain's take-off was fuelled partly by colonies whose own development was deliberately suppressed — the ladder was pulled up behind the climbers
The model was written by a colonial administrator

questions.question: The model's treatment of high mass consumption is criticised because:
options: Consumption cannot be measured
No country has ever reached the stage
Mass consumption always precedes take-off
It crowns consumption as the summit with no stage for sustainability — written before anyone asked whether the planet could host eight billion mass consumers

subtopics.title: Reading Real Places With Both Models

questions.question: South Africa's Rostow preconditions arrived with:
options: The mineral revolution — railways and ports built after 1870 to serve diamonds and gold
The 1994 elections
The founding of the JSE alone
Post-war motor assembly plants

questions.question: Apartheid is described as core-periphery engineering by law because:
options: It abolished the core entirely
The homelands were designed as labour reservoirs — peripheries whose backwash of migrant workers fed the mining core
It moved all industry to the periphery
It ended migration between regions

questions.question: Post-1994 projects like the Coega industrial development zone and the Maputo corridor are best read as:
options: Rostow's traditional society stage
Backwash effects
Attempts to build new cores in the periphery and pump spread effects outward
High mass consumption

questions.question: The essay synthesis comparing the two models is:
options: Both models describe timelines
Both models describe maps
Core-periphery assumes all regions develop together
Rostow describes a timeline and assumes regions ride it together; core-periphery describes a map and insists they do not — use one for history, the other for geography, and criticise both

subtopics.title: Five Boxes Every Plan Must Tick

questions.question: The inspector who checks whether we are 'burning the roof beams to warm today's room' stands for:
options: Sustainability — meeting today's needs without robbing future generations of theirs
Economic development
Spatial development
Appropriate scale

questions.question: The village given a giant high-tech water plant it cannot repair received:
options: Appropriate technology
A monument, not development — the solution failed the fit test of appropriate scale
Sustainable development
A spread effect

questions.question: The fifth inspector, who checks the map, is asking:
options: Whether the country's borders are correct
Whether GDP is growing
Whether development is spreading spatially or piling up in one favoured corner
Whether the plan is written down

subtopics.title: The Magnet and the Empty Edges

questions.question: In the magnet picture, the iron filings sliding inward are:
options: People, capital and resources drawn from the periphery to the core — the backwash
Spread effects reaching the periphery
Government grants
Exports leaving the country

questions.question: A migrant worker's remittances building a house back home in the Eastern Cape is an example of:
options: Backwash
A spread effect — value trickling from core to periphery
Cumulative causation
Take-off

questions.question: Government planning described as 'plumbing' means:
options: Building water infrastructure in the core
Blocking all migration
Trying to widen the spread pipes and narrow the backwash drain — for example bolting a new magnet like Coega onto the periphery
Increasing taxes in the periphery

questions.question: The 'three zoom levels' answer applies core-periphery at:
options: Farm, town and city
Past, present and future
Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Global (North and South), national (Gauteng and former homelands) and local (office-tower core and township edge)

questions.question: In the aeroplane picture, the ground crew laying railways, building ports and opening banks represents:
options: The preconditions for take-off
Traditional society
The drive to maturity
High mass consumption

questions.question: The plane's speed 'generating its own lift' captures:
options: The role of foreign aid
Take-off — growth becoming self-sustaining as manufacturing multiplies and investment passes about 10 per cent of income
The move to services
Population growth

questions.question: 'Some planes were fuelled by siphoning other planes' tanks' is the criticism that:
options: Rostow ignored technology
All economies grow at the same speed
Colonial powers took off partly on the resources and suppressed markets of their colonies — a history the model ignores
Aid creates dependency

questions.question: The South African observation that defeats a one-staircase model is:
options: The country never built railways
The economy has no service sector
Take-off happened before the mineral revolution
Apartheid deliberately kept millions of people off the flight for decades, and no stage model has a stage for that
